title: Why the Southeast is Burning
author: Zachary Handlos
content:
![](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732054/original/file-20260423-57-aski7q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&rect=221%2C246%2C2675%2C1752&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)Fire
crews responded to dozens of wildfires burning in Georgia and northern Florida
on April 23, 2026. Georgia Department of Natural Resources.

Large parts of the southeastern U.S. are in the midst of an exceptional
drought, and it is [fueling dozens of
wildfires](https://cdn.theconversation.com/static_files/files/4193/NIFC-
Southern_Area-042426.pdf) in
[Florida](https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/state/2026/04/24/where-
florida-wildfires-road-closures/89768151007/) and
[Georgia](https://gatrees.org/current-wildfire-information-and-resources).

One of those wildfires, in [southeastern Georgia’s Brantley
County](https://abcnews.com/US/georgia-wildfire-destroys-dozens-homes-
spreads-5000-acres/story?id=132268739), had [damaged about 90
homes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pZZ272wuX8E) by April 24, 2026, and
officials said about 800 other homes were at risk. Another fire near the
Georgia-Florida border had [burned more than 30,000
acres](https://gatrees.org/current-wildfire-information-and-resources) and
about 35 structures, and more than 180 homes at considered risk. The smoke
from the blazes [triggered air quality
alerts](https://www.fox5atlanta.com/news/code-orange-air-quality-alert-place-
metro-atlanta-due-smoke) in Atlanta, in the north-central part of the state.

Why is a region of the U.S. more often known for [thunderstorms and humidity
in spring](https://statesummaries.ncics.org/chapter/ga/) seeing so many
wildfires?

[![A forested area with a burned-out vehicle, burned trees and gray ash
covering
everything.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732055/original/file-20260423-57-ckqpm0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732055/original/file-20260423-57-ckqpm0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)A
fire near the Florida-Georgia line had burned nearly 30,000 acres by April 23,
2026, leaving ash behind. [Georgia Department of Natural
Resources.](https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/USWildfires/b55bbcb52acd43ad9b58d7fd4c5565db/photo)

I [teach meteorology at the Georgia Institute of
Technology](https://handlos.eas.gatech.edu/), including how weather patterns
can lead to conditions conducive to wildfires. Here’s what’s happening to
drive these conditions.

**Key ingredients for a wildfire**

Wildfires need [a few key ingredients](https://www.noaa.gov/noaa-
wildfire/wildfire-climate-connection) to spread: low relative humidity, dry
fuels and strong winds.

Much of the Southeast has been in a [drought since July
2025](https://www.drought.gov/drought-status-updates/drought-status-update-
southeast-2026-04-16). From mid-March to mid-April 2026, the region saw less
than a quarter of its normal precipitation for that time of year.

![A U.S. map showing very dry conditions over much of the eastern U.S., the
Southwest and the Great
Plains.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732039/original/file-20260423-57-21tgyh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)A
map showing how far above or below average precipitation has been in each
region from mid-March to mid-April 2026 shows just how dry much of the U.S.
Southeast has been.  
[Drought.gov](https://www.drought.gov/)

As a result, the U.S. Drought Monitor classified most of this region in
[“extreme” or “exceptional”
drought](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/CurrentMap/StateDroughtMonitor.aspx?southeast)
by mid-April.

![In the map of the Southeast, an area of exceptional drought stretches from
the Florida Panhandle to central coastal Georgia. much of the rest of the two
states are extreme
drought.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732056/original/file-20260423-57-6gru0v.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)A
map of the U.S. Southeast as of April 21, 2026, shows exceptional drought
across the Georgia-Florida border area and extreme drought in many other
areas.  
[Brian Fuchs, National Drought Mitigation Center/U.S. Drought
Monitor](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/CurrentMap/StateDroughtMonitor.aspx?southeast)

Part of the reason for the lack of rainfall has been a persistent high-
pressure system over the Southeast.

[High-pressure
systems](https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/about/k-12-education/weather-
forecasting/what-are-high-and-low-pressure-systems) are areas where air aloft
sinks toward the surface, preventing clouds and precipitation from forming.
The Southeast high-pressure system resulted from the presence of [a “ridge” in
the jet stream](https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/upper-air-charts/basic-wave-
patterns), a northward bend in this fast current of air several miles above
Earth’s surface.

Another consequence of this high pressure has been the presence of generally
southeast winds, which have transported warm and fairly dry air into the area.

The relative humidity – a measure of the amount of moisture in the air
relative to the maximum amount the air can contain at its actual air
temperature – has also been very low due to warmer-than-usual temperatures and
lower-than-usual moisture.

[![A weather map shows the high-pressure system over the Southeast keeping
conditions
dry.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732040/original/file-20260423-57-s4f7d8.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/732040/original/file-20260423-57-s4f7d8.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)A
weather map from the Global Forecast System for April 23, 2026, shows the
forecasted low-pressure (red L) and high-pressure (blue H) systems. [Pivotal
Weather](https://home.pivotalweather.com/)

As a result of these conditions, [trees, grass and leaves dry
out](https://www.noaa.gov/noaa-wildfire/wildfire-climate-connection) and can
quickly become fuel for wildfires. That kind of dry fuel is widespread
throughout rural areas of Georgia and north Florida.

Once a fire starts, whether from lightning, power lines or other human
sources, strong winds can spread it rapidly in these conditions. Georgia fire
officials said the largest fire in mid-April, near the Florida state line,
started with a [spark from welding equipment](https://gatrees.org/current-
wildfire-information-and-resources/) that ignited surrounding vegetation. They
believe a mylar balloon hitting a power line sparked the fire that burned
dozens of homes in Brantley County.

**What’s ahead for the region?**

As global temperatures rise, the [frequency of drought conditions in the
Southeast will
increase](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-07/documents/southeast_fact_sheet.pdf).
This, in combination with [less soil moisture content in the
summer](https://cpo.noaa.gov/nca5-drought-and-climate-change-in-10-maps/),
could be conducive for increased wildfire activity.

Wildfires do eventually burn out. It takes a combination of help from the
atmosphere, with moisture to douse them, and firefighters clearing away dry
fuel to stop their spread.

Georgia and Florida may get a reprieve soon from the weather, as multiple low-
pressure systems are forecast for the region in late April and early May that
could bring rainfall. In the meantime, more than half of Georgia’s counties
are [under a state of emergency](https://gov.georgia.gov/press-
releases/2026-04-22/gov-kemp-declares-state-emergency-response-south-georgia-
wildfires), as several agencies battle the flames to protect homes with
helicopters in the air and [scores of
firefighters](https://www.facebook.com/photo?fbid=1423245599827492&set=pcb.1423246663160719)
on the ground.
